title: Caching fundamentals
scopeHtml:
Scope: cache-aside, read/write-through, write-back, eviction, TTL, invalidation and hit-ratio math.

Scope: cache-aside, read/write-through, write-back, eviction, TTL, invalidation and hit-ratio math.

notes.title: Why caching works
notes.html:
A cache is a small, fast copy of data that is slow to get from its real home. It works because access is skewed: a few items get most of the reads (the 80/20 rule, often even 95/5). Keep those few in RAM and most requests never touch the database.

Numbers to remember: a Redis GET over a LAN takes about 0.2 to 1 ms. A Postgres indexed read is about 1 to 5 ms when warm and 10 ms or more under load. A cross-region call is 50 to 150 ms. The cache wins on latency and, more importantly, protects the database from load.

Worked example. A product page gets 20,000 reads/s. Postgres can comfortably do about 5,000 simple reads/s. With a 95% hit ratio, only 1,000 reads/s reach Postgres. The cache turned an impossible load into an easy one without touching the database.

Industry examples. Facebook runs one of the largest Memcached fleets (their "Scaling Memcache" paper) so that MySQL sees a small fraction of reads. Twitter and Instagram cache timelines and counters in Redis/Memcached. Netflix EVCache holds hot metadata close to every region.

Everyday analogy. Keeping your most used spices on the kitchen counter instead of walking to the store each time.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding a cache with no idea of the hit ratio or what is hot. A cache for uniformly random access is nearly useless.
  • Forgetting that a cache is a second source of truth that can disagree with the first.
  • Caching to hide a missing index. Fix the query first.

notes.title: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
notes.html:
The application owns the logic: read the cache; on a miss read the database, then put the result in the cache. Writes go to the database and then delete (or update) the cache key.

def get_user(uid):
    v = redis.get(f"user:{uid}")
    if v: return json.loads(v)
    row = db.query("select * from users where id=%s", uid)
    redis.set(f"user:{uid}", json.dumps(row), ex=300)   # TTL 5 min
    return row

def update_user(uid, data):
    db.update(uid, data)
    redis.delete(f"user:{uid}")      # delete, do not set: see race below

Why chosen. Simple, the cache holds only what is asked for, and a dead cache only slows things (the DB still answers). Alternative: read-through (cache library loads for you). It breaks with a cold cache (every first read is slow) and with a race: reader A reads old DB value, writer updates DB and deletes key, reader A then writes the old value into the cache. It stays stale until the TTL. Delete-on-write plus a short TTL limits the damage. Easy to change later: a two-way door.

Industry examples. Most Redis usage in the wild is cache-aside. Facebook's Memcache deletes keys on write and uses "leases" to fix the race above.

Everyday analogy. You check your notes first; if the answer is missing you look it up in the book and write it in your notes.

Common interview traps.

  • Updating the cache on write instead of deleting: two concurrent writers can leave the older value last.
  • Not setting a TTL, so a missed invalidation lives forever.

notes.title: Read-through, write-through, write-behind
notes.html:
These move the caching logic from your code into the cache layer.

  • Read-through: the cache itself loads from the database on a miss. The app only talks to the cache.
  • Write-through: every write goes to the cache and the database synchronously, and returns when both succeed. Reads are always fresh, writes are slower (two hops).
  • Write-back (write-behind): write to the cache, return immediately, flush to the database later in batches. Very fast writes, but if the cache node dies before the flush, you lose data.
Pattern Write latency Data loss risk Typical use
Cache-aside DB speed None General purpose
Write-through DB + cache None Read-heavy, freshness needed
Write-back Cache speed Yes, on crash Counters, likes, metrics

Worked example. A "like" counter takes 50,000 increments/s on a viral post. Writing each to Postgres would melt one row. Write-back: Redis INCR and a worker flushes the total every 5 s, so Postgres gets 0.2 writes/s. Cost: up to 5 s of likes lost if Redis dies without persistence.

Industry examples. CPU caches use write-back. DynamoDB DAX is a write-through cache. Many view-count systems (YouTube-style) buffer counts and flush in batches.

Everyday analogy. Write-through: sign the register and the ledger together. Write-back: scribble on a sticky note and update the ledger tonight.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing write-back for money or orders. Never for data you cannot lose.
  • Ignoring ordering: batched flushes can reorder writes unless keyed carefully.

notes.title: Eviction policies
notes.html:
When the cache is full, it must throw something away. The policy decides what.

  • LRU (least recently used): evict what was untouched longest. The default good choice.
  • LFU (least frequently used): evict the least popular. Better when a few items are hot for a long time; resists one-time scans.
  • FIFO / random: cheap, rarely best.
  • TTL-based: evict expired first.

Redis config: maxmemory 8gb and maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (cache use), or volatile-lru (only keys with TTL), allkeys-lfu, noeviction (returns errors when full, for data stores). Redis LRU is approximated by sampling (maxmemory-samples, default 5), not an exact list.

Worked example. 10M items of 1 KB = 10 GB of data but only 4 GB of RAM. If access is skewed so that the hottest 3M items take 90% of reads, LRU keeps them and the hit ratio is near 90%. A big one-time scan (a batch job reading everything) can flush the hot set from plain LRU; LFU or a separate cache for scans avoids this.

Industry examples. Memcached uses a segmented LRU per slab class. Redis added LFU in 4.0. Caffeine (Java) uses W-TinyLFU, a strong modern admission policy.

Everyday analogy. A small desk: the paper you have not touched for months goes back in the cabinet first.

Common interview traps.

  • Using noeviction for a cache and then seeing OOM write errors.
  • Not leaving headroom: Redis fork for snapshots can double memory briefly; keep maxmemory around 60 to 75% of RAM.

notes.title: TTL and invalidation
notes.html:
"There are only two hard things: cache invalidation and naming things." Invalidation is making sure the cache does not serve data that is wrong for too long.

Options, from simplest to most precise:

  1. TTL only: accept staleness up to the TTL (30 s for a feed, 5 min for a profile, 24 h for static config). Add jitter (random +/-10%) so keys do not all expire together.
  2. Delete on write: the writer removes the key after the DB commit.
  3. Event-driven: DB changes (CDC, see the outbox notes) publish events, a consumer deletes keys. Works across services.
  4. Versioned keys: user:42:v17. A change bumps the version; old keys just age out. No delete race.

Decision gravity. Choose staleness tolerance per data type, not globally. Prices and inventory need seconds; avatars can be hours. TTL-only is easy to reverse; a CDC-based invalidation pipeline is an investment that is hard to rip out.

Industry examples. Facebook tails the MySQL binlog to invalidate Memcache (the McSqueal daemon). CDNs use purge APIs plus TTL (Cloudflare, Fastly).

Everyday analogy. Milk in the fridge: a date stamp (TTL), or you throw it out the moment you buy a fresh carton (delete on write).

Common interview traps.

  • Delete before the DB commit: a reader can refill the old value in between.
  • Same TTL on all keys, producing an expiry cliff (see avalanche in the next notes).
  • Caching "not found" forever; use a short TTL for negatives.

notes.title: Hit-ratio math
notes.html:
Hit ratio = hits / (hits + misses). Average latency = hit_ratio x cache_latency + (1 - hit_ratio) x db_latency. And DB load = total QPS x (1 - hit_ratio).

Worked example. Cache 1 ms, DB 20 ms, 10,000 QPS.

Hit ratio Avg latency DB QPS
80% 0.8 + 4.0 = 4.8 ms 2,000
95% 0.95 + 1.0 = 1.95 ms 500
99% 0.99 + 0.2 = 1.19 ms 100

Going from 95% to 99% cuts DB load 5x. The last few points matter hugely, so measure the miss rate, not the hit rate. Sizing: if the working set is 6 GB and you give 3 GB, expect the hit ratio to fall sharply. Redis metrics: keyspace_hits, keyspace_misses, evicted_keys; high evictions plus falling hit ratio means too little memory.

Industry examples. Facebook reports hit rates well above 90% and still focuses on the miss tail since it sets database capacity. CDN offload percent is the same metric.

Everyday analogy. A library lending desk: if 99 of 100 questions are answered from the front desk, the archive staff barely work.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting the hit ratio without the key-space size or working-set size.
  • Forgetting that a cold start (after a restart) has a hit ratio near 0 and can crush the DB; warm caches before shifting traffic.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A cache protects the database and cuts latency because access is skewed; always estimate hit ratio and DB load.
  • Cache-aside is the default: read cache, fall back to DB, delete on write, always set a TTL.
  • Write-through is fresh but slower; write-back is fastest but can lose data.
  • Use LRU/LFU with maxmemory headroom; avoid noeviction for caches.
  • Invalidate by TTL with jitter, delete-on-write, events, or versioned keys; pick per data type.
  • Hit-ratio math: DB QPS = QPS x miss rate; 95% to 99% is a 5x drop in DB load.

questions.promptHtml: Why does adding a cache in front of a database help, and when would it not help?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you reason about access skew and hit ratio instead of saying "cache = faster".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Access is skewed: a few keys take most reads. I keep those in RAM, so most requests never reach the database. That cuts latency (about 1 ms vs 5-20 ms) and, more importantly, cuts database load to QPS x miss rate. It does not help when access is near-uniform over a key space far bigger than the cache, or when the real problem is a missing index.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three numbers drive everything: hit ratio h, cache latency Lc, DB latency Ld. Average latency = h*Lc + (1-h)Ld. DB load = QPS(1-h). With 20,000 reads/s and a DB that does about 5,000/s, you need h >= 75% just to survive, and you want margin, so aim for 95%.

20k QPS -> cache (95% hit) -> 1k QPS -> Postgres (limit ~5k)

Skew is why this works: if 5% of items take 90% of reads, a cache holding 5% of the data gets about 90% hits. If every key is equally likely and the cache holds 5% of keys, the hit ratio is about 5%.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding a cache with no measurement of hit ratio or working-set size.
  • Caching to hide a slow query that needs an index.
  • Forgetting the cache is a second source of truth that can disagree with the DB.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is the cost of a cache? -> Staleness, invalidation logic, a new failure mode, memory cost, cold-start risk.
  2. Which metric do you watch? -> Miss rate and evictions, since DB capacity is set by the misses.
  3. When is a cache harmful? -> Uniform access, tiny datasets that fit in DB memory anyway, data needing strict freshness.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "it is faster". The senior answer does the load math, names the skew assumption, and says what happens to the DB when the cache is cold.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams add Redis, see no DB relief, and discover a 20% hit ratio because keys include a per-request timestamp.

questions.promptHtml: In cache-aside, why do we delete the cache key on write instead of updating it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic race question; shows you know concurrent reader/writer interleavings.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cache-aside means the app reads cache, on miss reads the DB and fills the cache. On write I commit to the DB and then delete the key. Updating the cache instead lets two concurrent writers leave the older value last. Deleting is idempotent: the next read reloads from the DB. A TTL still bounds the rare stale case.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Update race: writer A sets DB=1, writer B sets DB=2, but cache writes arrive B then A, so cache=1 while DB=2 until TTL. With delete, both just remove the key and the reader refills from the DB.

Remaining race with delete: reader R reads old DB value v1, writer W commits v2 and deletes the key, R then writes v1 into the cache. It is rare because the reader's DB read plus cache write must straddle the writer's commit plus delete. TTL bounds it. Facebook closes it with leases.

def update_user(uid, data):
    db.update(uid, data)          # commit first
    redis.delete(f"user:{uid}")   # then delete

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Deleting before the DB commit: a reader refills the old value in the gap.
  • No TTL, so one missed invalidation lives forever.
  • Believing delete makes it fully consistent; it makes it eventually consistent.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the delete fails? -> Retry via a queue or rely on a short TTL; alert on repeated failures.
  2. Why not write-through? -> It is a different pattern with its own cost (two hops on every write); fine when freshness matters and reads dominate.
  3. How do you close the reader race fully? -> Leases or versioned keys, or CDC-driven invalidation with versions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "delete is simpler". Senior: draws both interleavings, names the residual race, and picks TTL or leases as the bound.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A profile service updated the cache on write; two quick edits left the old name visible for the full 1-hour TTL.

questions.contextHtml: A product-detail API serves 12,000 reads/s at peak. The Postgres replica does about 4,000 of these reads/s with p99 under 20 ms; beyond that p99 climbs past 200 ms. A cache read costs 1 ms, a DB read 15 ms. The product asks: "What hit ratio do we need, and what is the average latency?" The team proposes a 5-minute TTL on every product.
questions.promptHtml: Do the math and tell me whether a 90% hit ratio is enough.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Caching will make it faster, 90% is great." No DB QPS calculation, so it misses that 90% leaves 1,200/s, fine, but a cold start or 60% hit ratio would not be.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 12k the peak or the average? What is the key-space size and the skew (do the top 5% of products take most traffic)? How stale may a product be? Is there a cold-start path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, but the safe first step is to measure the real hit ratio from keyspace_hits/misses on a shadow cache.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) skewed access, so 90%+ is plausible; (b) a long tail of rarely read products drags it to 70-80%; (c) per-user keys fragment the cache.
  4. How I'd verify each: Sample 1 hour of request logs, compute top-N share, simulate an LRU of the proposed size.
  5. Root cause / math: DB QPS = 12,000 x (1-h). Limit 4,000 means h >= 66.7% minimum. At 90%: 1,200/s. At 95%: 600/s. Average latency at 90%: 0.9 + 1.5 = 2.4 ms; at 95%: 0.95 + 0.75 = 1.7 ms. So 90% survives with 3x headroom, but only in steady state.
  6. Fix: Size memory for the working set; add TTL jitter; pre-warm before cutover; alert if miss rate x QPS approaches 50% of DB capacity.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards on miss rate, evictions and DB QPS with the 4k limit drawn on it.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not size for the average hit ratio. The cold-start case is 100% misses = 12,000/s, three times the DB limit, so warm-up is part of the design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Traffic doubles to 24k/s? -> Need h >= 83% to stay at 4k; at 90% the DB sees 2,400, still OK, so cache holds but headroom halves.
  • Cache node restarts? -> 12k/s hits DB for a while; need replicas, warm-up or a local cache layer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team sized the DB for a 95% hit ratio, then a deploy changed the cache key format. Hit ratio went to 0 for minutes and the DB fell over; the math had been right, the cold path was never tested.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: gives a hit ratio with no DB QPS math.
  • Hire: computes DB load and latency correctly and mentions cold start.
  • Strong hire: also questions skew, sizes memory by working set, and sets alerts tied to DB capacity.

questions.contextHtml: A live-streaming app has two features: (1) a "likes" counter, up to 50,000 increments/s on one viral stream; (2) a wallet balance for tipping creators, about 300 writes/s. An engineer proposes write-back (Redis first, flush to MySQL every 5 s) for both "to keep MySQL cool". Redis runs as a primary plus one async replica, AOF everysec.
questions.promptHtml: Do you agree? Which pattern for each?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Write-back is fastest so use it for both," or "Never use write-back." Neither separates data you can lose from data you cannot.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How much loss is tolerable for likes (seconds? a count of 1,000)? Is the wallet balance the source of truth or a display copy? Is there an audit trail? What is the RPO for each?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; this is a design review. I would block write-back for the wallet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Likes: write-back fits; the row is a hot-row bottleneck (50k/s on one MySQL row would serialize on a row lock). Wallet: money must be durable and exactly-once.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load-test a single-row UPDATE counter = counter + 1 for the ceiling (likely a few thousand/s); check Redis failover loss on a kill test.
  5. Root cause / reasoning: Write-back loses whatever is not flushed if Redis dies. Async replica plus AOF everysec can lose about 1 s or more of acknowledged writes. For likes, losing 5-6 s of 50k/s = about 300,000 increments out of millions is cosmetic. For a wallet, any loss is a ledger break.
  6. Fix: Likes: Redis INCR, flusher writes totals every 5 s (idempotent set of absolute value, not delta replay). Wallet: write to the DB transactionally (write-through or just DB-first and cache-aside for reads), with an idempotency key per tip.
  7. Prevention: Test the Redis-kill scenario; label each data class with a loss budget.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use write-back for orders, money or anything with legal audit. Cost of my choice: wallet writes pay DB latency, which at 300/s is trivial.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Counter must be exact for billing sponsors? -> Then log events durably (Kafka) and aggregate; the display counter stays approximate.
  • Flusher crashes after read, before write? -> Write absolute values so a rerun is idempotent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "views" counter in write-back lost 40 minutes of counts after a failover; nobody cared. The same team later reused the pattern for coupon redemptions and double-issued coupons.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: same pattern for both.
  • Hire: splits by loss tolerance and names the durability gap.
  • Strong hire: also notes the hot-row limit, idempotent flushing and idempotency keys for money.

questions.contextHtml:
Users report that after changing their email, the old email shows for up to an hour, roughly 1 in 300 updates. The code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void updateEmail(long uid, String email) {
    cache.delete("user:" + uid);          // invalidate first
    db.updateEmail(uid, email);           // then commit
}
User getUser(long uid) {
    User u = cache.get("user:" + uid);
    if (u == null) { u = db.load(uid); cache.set("user:" + uid, u, 3600); }
    return u;
}
fun updateEmail(uid: Long, email: String) {
    cache.delete("user:$uid")             // invalidate first
    db.updateEmail(uid, email)            // then commit
}
fun getUser(uid: Long): User =
    cache.get("user:$uid") ?: db.load(uid).also { cache.set("user:$uid", it, 3600) }

The profile page makes three concurrent requests (header, settings, API) so reads overlap writes often.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain the interleaving, fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a lock" or "lower the TTL". It treats symptoms and misses the ordering of delete vs commit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the DB read from a replica (lag adds a second window)? Is the TTL needed at all? Is there a transaction wrapper that commits later than the method returns?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop the TTL for user keys to 60 s to cap the damage.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) delete-before-commit race; (b) replica lag on the refill read; (c) transaction commits after the method returns (delete runs before commit).
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a log with key, DB version and timestamp on refill; compare with commit time; check pg_stat_replication lag.
  5. Root cause: Timeline: W deletes key; R misses, reads old email from the DB (not yet committed); W commits; R sets old value with TTL 3600. Stale for an hour.
  6. Fix: Commit first, then delete (after the transaction really committed, e.g. in an after-commit hook). For the residual race add a delayed second delete (double delete after ~500 ms) or versioned keys. Reads that refill should use the primary or a version check.
  7. Prevention: A concurrency test that interleaves read and write with a latch; a lint or review rule: "invalidate after commit".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on a global lock, since it serializes the hot read path for one rare race.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Delete fails after commit? -> Retry from an outbox or accept the TTL bound; shorten TTL for sensitive fields.
  • Multiple services read this user? -> CDC-driven invalidation instead of in-code delete.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "fixed" a similar bug with a lock, doubled p99 and still had stale reads, because the real window was an uncommitted transaction.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests only a lower TTL.
  • Hire: names delete-before-commit and flips the order.
  • Strong hire: also covers after-commit hooks, replica lag, double delete or versions.

questions.contextHtml: Checkout starts failing at 14:05 with 500s. App logs show: OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'. The Redis box has 16 GB RAM; config is maxmemory 14gb, maxmemory-policy noeviction. INFO shows used_memory 14.0G, evicted_keys 0, keyspace_hits falling and DB CPU at 85%. A new feature released at 13:30 caches search results with TTL 24 h.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase maxmemory" or "restart Redis". Restart empties the cache and moves the problem to the DB.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does this Redis hold only cache or also sessions and queues? What is the share of keys with TTL? What changed at 13:30?
  2. Immediate mitigation: CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (live, no restart) so writes succeed, then watch evicted_keys. If sessions live here too, use volatile-lru and check that cache keys carry TTLs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: New search-result keys with 24 h TTL filled the memory; big values; no headroom for fork/replication buffers.
  4. How I'd verify each: redis-cli --bigkeys, MEMORY USAGE key, INFO keyspace for key counts and avg TTL, INFO memory for fragmentation.
  5. Root cause: noeviction is right for a data store, wrong for a cache: when full it rejects writes instead of dropping cold keys. The new feature added unbounded keys with long TTL.
  6. Fix: Short term: switch policy. Long term: shorter TTL on search results (5-15 min), cap value size, set maxmemory to 60-75% of RAM for fork headroom, separate Redis instances for cache vs sessions.
  7. Prevention: Alert on used_memory/maxmemory > 80%, evicted_keys rate, and a pre-release check of key cardinality x size for new caches.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise maxmemory to 16 GB; a BGSAVE fork could then push the box into swap. I would not flush the cache.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sessions are in the same Redis? -> allkeys-lru could evict logins; use volatile-lru with TTLs on cache only, then split instances.
  • Hit ratio drops after the policy change? -> Expected for cold keys; check evictions vs working set, add memory if hot keys evict.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team copied a data-store Redis config for a cache cluster; the first traffic peak with a new feature produced a write outage that looked like a Redis bug.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts or raises memory.
  • Hire: changes the eviction policy and explains noeviction.
  • Strong hire: adds headroom reasoning, TTL discipline, instance separation, alerts.

questions.promptHtml: Compare cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-back. How do you choose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you map pattern to loss tolerance, freshness and who owns the loading logic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cache-aside: the app manages the cache, DB-speed writes, no loss. Read-through: the cache loads on a miss, the app only talks to the cache. Write-through: each write hits cache and DB synchronously, always fresh, slower writes. Write-back: ack from the cache, flush later, fastest but loses data on a crash. I default to cache-aside, use write-back only for data I can lose.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pattern        Write latency   Loss risk   Freshness     Owner of logic
Cache-aside    DB              none        TTL-bounded   app
Read-through   DB              none        TTL-bounded   cache lib
Write-through  DB + cache      none        fresh         cache lib
Write-back     cache           on crash    cache-first   cache + flusher

Write-back also risks reordering of batched flushes and needs idempotent absolute-value writes. Write-through doubles the write path, so it pays off only when reads need fresh values right after writes. Read-through is a code-structure choice: it centralises the loader and enables request collapsing.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Write-back for orders or money.
  • Write-through everywhere, paying double latency for data no one reads.
  • Calling read-through "a different cache"; it is the same cache with the loader moved.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which survives a cache outage best? -> Cache-aside; the DB still answers, just slower.
  2. How do you make write-back safer? -> Persistence (AOF), replicas, a durable log of increments, small flush windows.
  3. Where does write-through bite? -> Partial failure: cache write succeeds, DB fails (or reverse); define ordering and rollback.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists definitions. Senior: picks per data class by loss budget and freshness, and names partial-failure behaviour.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A write-through layer returned success when the cache write passed but the DB write timed out; reads showed data that did not exist.

questions.promptHtml: When would you choose LFU over LRU, and how does Redis actually implement LRU?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of scan pollution and of approximate algorithms in real systems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: LRU evicts what was untouched longest; it is a good default. A big one-time scan (batch job, crawler) touches everything once and flushes the hot set from plain LRU. LFU evicts the least frequently used, so a few long-lived hot items survive scans. Redis does not keep an exact LRU list; it samples maxmemory-samples keys (default 5) and evicts the best candidate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Exact LRU needs a linked list updated on every read, a lock and memory per key. Redis stores a small timestamp per key and samples, trading exactness for speed. Raising samples to 10 gets close to true LRU at some CPU cost. LFU (since Redis 4.0) keeps a logarithmic counter with decay (lfu-log-factor, lfu-decay-time) so old popularity fades. W-TinyLFU (Caffeine) adds an admission filter: a new item enters only if it looks more popular than the victim.

config: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using LRU for a cache that a nightly scan reads fully.
  • Using LFU for rapidly changing trends: old popular items stick unless decay is tuned.
  • volatile-* policies with keys that have no TTL: nothing is evictable, writes fail.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you run Redis --hotkeys? -> Only with an LFU policy.
  2. FIFO or random? -> Cheap, but ignores recency; rarely best.
  3. How do you protect against scan pollution without LFU? -> Separate cache or bypass the cache for batch reads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "LRU = recently used". Senior: explains sampling, scan pollution, decay, admission and how to test a policy against a recorded trace.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A nightly export evicted the whole product hot set; morning traffic hit a cold cache until 10 am.

questions.contextHtml: A PM says: "Search is slow. Just cache everything for 10 minutes." The catalogue API serves item title, image URL, price, stock count and seller rating at 8,000 QPS. Price changes happen about 50 times/hour and a wrong price shown at checkout is a legal complaint. Stock hits 0 for popular items several times a day, and overselling costs refunds.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond and what do you design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts one global 10-minute TTL, or refuses to cache. Neither extracts requirements per field.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which fields can be stale and for how long? Is the cached price used at checkout or only for display? What is the source of truth for stock? How many distinct items (key space)? Who invalidates, the catalogue service only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Show price at checkout always from the DB (cache for display only); that removes the legal risk at once.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Titles/images tolerate hours; rating tolerates minutes; price tolerates seconds with delete-on-write; stock needs no cache or a very short one.
  4. How I'd verify each: Pull change frequency per field from DB audit logs; measure what share of the 8k QPS touches each field.
  5. Root cause / reasoning: One TTL for all fields forces the strictest requirement or breaks it. Split into cache entries by volatility.
  6. Fix: item:static TTL 6 h + jitter; item:price delete on write (event from the pricing service) with TTL 60 s as a bound; rating TTL 10 min; stock read from an atomic counter store, not the generic cache.
  7. Prevention: A data-class table (field, owner, staleness budget, invalidation method) agreed with the PM; a metric for stale-served age.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cache stock decisions; display counts like "only 3 left" can be approximate, the reservation cannot. Splitting keys costs more round trips; MGET or a pipeline fixes that.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Price changes jump to 5,000/hour (sale)? -> Switch to event-driven invalidation through CDC; the TTL stays only as a safety net.
  • Another team also caches price? -> Publish invalidation events, not direct deletes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "cache everything 10 min" rollout shipped, and a flash-sale price correction stayed wrong for the full 10 minutes; support handled hundreds of tickets.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: single TTL or no caching.
  • Hire: splits by field and uses delete-on-write for price.
  • Strong hire: also keeps checkout off the cache, quantifies change rates and defines a staleness budget.

questions.contextHtml: You are moving a 40 GB self-managed Redis (single primary) to a managed cluster. Traffic is 25,000 reads/s at 96% hit ratio; the DB handles 3,000 reads/s comfortably, 6,000 at the edge. Cutting the app over directly will start the new cluster empty. Last quarter a cache flush pushed DB CPU to 100% for 12 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration so users see nothing.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch the connection string at 2 am." That sends 25k/s to a DB with a 6k edge.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can keys be rebuilt from the DB? Any non-cache data (sessions, locks) in this Redis? Does the client support the cluster protocol? Multi-key commands or Lua in use?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Define a rollback: the old Redis stays up and the flag flips back in under a minute.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cold cache will cause a miss storm (25k/s vs 6k DB edge); cluster mode breaks multi-key ops; key design leaves a hot slot.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the app against a staging cluster with a replayed trace; grep code for multi-key commands; redis-cli --cluster check.
  5. Root cause / math: Cold = 100% misses = 25,000/s, 8x the DB's comfortable level. Need hit ratio >= 88% to stay at 3,000/s, and >= 76% to stay under the 6k edge.
  6. Fix: Phase 1: dual-write (writes and invalidations go to both). Phase 2: shadow reads to the new cluster to warm it, no serving. Phase 3: ramp 1% to 5% to 25% to 100% of reads by flag while watching DB QPS and hit ratio; hold if DB QPS rises above 4k. Optionally bulk-copy hot keys with redis-cli --scan plus DUMP/RESTORE or use a replication tool. Phase 4: stop dual-write, keep the old one for a week.
  7. Prevention: Run the plan in a game day; keep a per-stage abort criterion written down.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not copy an RDB snapshot and assume it is warm and consistent: writes in the gap are lost. Dual-write costs complexity and a short window of inconsistency, acceptable for cache data.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ramp stalls at 25% with hit ratio 80%? -> Pause; warm longer or add a local cache to absorb the hottest keys.
  • Cluster rejects a Lua script? -> Use hash tags to co-locate keys or rewrite the script per key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration that skipped warm-up passed all tests and still tripped a DB alert at 2 am; the ramp-by-flag version of the same move later went unnoticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: direct cutover.
  • Hire: warm-up and gradual traffic shift with rollback.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the miss storm against DB limits, handles dual-write and cluster constraints, defines abort criteria.

questions.contextHtml: Support reports that about 0.2% of users see an old plan after upgrading, until their cache entry expires after 24 h. Logs show writes: UPDATE plans ... COMMIT then DEL plan:u:8812, both successful. The DB is Postgres with a streaming read replica; reads for the cache refill go to the replica. pg_stat_replication shows replay lag of 50 ms normally and 2-4 s during a nightly batch. Red herring: the CDN also caches static assets for 24 h.
questions.promptHtml: Explain how stale data is cached even though the delete always runs after commit, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "TTL is too long" or blames the CDN. It does not find the replica-lag refill.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which DB serves the refill read? Does the plan endpoint set cache headers? Are stale users concentrated in the batch window?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cut the TTL for plan keys to 60 s and delete affected keys for known users.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) replica lag on refill; (b) reader/writer race; (c) a second writer path that skips the delete; (d) CDN (check Cache-Control and Age).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the replica LSN or pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() at refill; correlate stale users with batch time; grep all writers of plans.
  5. Root cause: Writer commits on the primary and deletes the key. A reader arrives within the lag window, misses, loads the pre-update row from the lagging replica and caches it for 24 h. The delete already happened, so nothing removes the stale value.
  6. Fix: Short term: TTL 60 s for this key class and refill from the primary for keys deleted in the last few seconds. Long term: version column in the row; cache stores (version, value) and refill rejects values older than a version hint; or delayed second delete after max lag; or CDC-driven invalidation that fires after the replica applies the change.
  7. Prevention: Alert on replica lag above 500 ms; test with injected lag; metric "cache refilled from lagging replica".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not move all reads to the primary; that loses the point of the replica. The version check adds one column but removes a class of bugs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Reads must use replicas for cost? -> Use the delayed second delete with delay greater than the 99th percentile lag.
  • Many services read this key? -> Publish a versioned invalidation event.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "random" 0.1% staleness bug was traced to a nightly job that raised replica lag; the fix was a 5-line version check.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only lowers TTL.
  • Hire: identifies replica lag as the refill source of stale data.
  • Strong hire: provides versioned refill or delayed delete, detection metrics and discusses cost.

questions.contextHtml: A recommendation cache: 200M items x 2 KB = 400 GB of data; the hot set (items read in the last day) is about 60 GB. Managed Redis costs about 8 USD per GB-month (verify). Current config: 200 GB cache, hit ratio 91%, 40,000 reads/s, DB load 3,600/s on a cluster that scales at about 1,500 reads/s per 1,000 USD/month. Finance wants a 30% cost cut. Metrics: evicted_keys 2,000/s, p99 miss path 80 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Where is the money best spent: cache memory or DB capacity? Show numbers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Shrink the cache, it is too big" or "buy more cache" without computing the marginal effect on DB load.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the reuse distance distribution, i.e. the hit ratio at 100/150/200 GB? Which items are evicted: hot or one-off? Is TTL reducing the working set? Any compression potential?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is optimization.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 140 GB of the 200 GB is cold tail yet 2,000 evictions/s suggests churn from one-time reads; LRU thrash from scans; values compressible.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay a trace through a cache simulator (varying size); sample evicted keys' age; test compression (e.g. zstd) on 1000 values.
  5. Root cause / math: Cache cost today: 200 x 8 = 1,600 USD/month. DB cost for 3,600 reads/s = 3,600/1,500 x 1,000 = 2,400 USD/month. Cutting the cache to 100 GB may drop hit ratio from 91% to, say, 86% (simulate): DB load 5,600/s = 3,733 USD/month, saving 800 on cache but adding 1,333 on the DB: a loss. Conversely, adding 60 GB (480 USD) that lifts hit ratio to 94% saves 1,600/s = 1,067 USD of DB: a win.
  6. Fix: Pick the size at the knee of the hit-ratio curve; enable admission (LFU or TinyLFU) to stop one-hit items taking space; compress values (2 KB to ~800 B halves memory for the same hit ratio); shorter TTL on long-tail.
  7. Prevention: Track "marginal DB cost per GB of cache" on the dashboard; re-run the simulation quarterly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cut memory based on average utilisation; the cost lives in the miss tail and the DB. Compression costs CPU and latency per read (sub-ms), fine for this path.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• DB is already at capacity? -> Misses are expensive, so spend on cache first.
  • Traffic skew shifts (new trend)? -> Re-simulate; an LFU with decay adapts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cost-cutting resize of a cache saved 700 USD/month and raised DB spend by 3,000; the dashboard only showed cache cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cuts cache for savings without effect on DB.
  • Hire: compares cache cost against DB cost using hit-ratio change.
  • Strong hire: uses a trace simulation, admission policy and compression, and states the marginal cost per GB.
